chapters.title: Phased-array antenna, direct-to-cell engineering, and patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## The Aperture Problem and How Avellan Solved It

Avellan and his chief scientist filed the company's first patent claims in 2017. The foundational insight: a sufficiently large phased-array antenna could generate enough effective isotropic radiated power to close a wideband LTE link with a standard handset. The phased array acts simultaneously as spatially directed transmitter and steerable receiver, electronically forming and moving beams without mechanical articulation. Larger aperture means greater antenna gain to trade against the orbital distance penalty.

## BlueWalker 3: Demonstrating the Principle at Scale

The physical ambition of that wager became visible to the world on 10 November 2022, when the BlueWalker 3 prototype completed its antenna deployment in orbit. The array spanned [693 square feet—64.4 square metres](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220908005651/en/AST-SpaceMobile-Announces-BlueWalker-3-the-Largest-Commercial-Communications-Array-Ever-Deployed-to-Low-Earth-Orbit)—making it the largest commercial communications array ever deployed to low Earth orbit. It had been stowed during the September 2022 Falcon 9 launch inside a volume little larger than an industrial refrigerator. Once on orbit, 148-micron panels unfolded autonomously, generating solar power on the Sun-facing side and transmitting and receiving cellular signals through the antenna elements facing Earth.

BlueWalker 3's link budget performance validated internal projections and materially de-risked the full BlueBird production commitment that followed. The satellite completed voice calls over standard LTE on unmodified smartphones and by April 2023 demonstrated 5G connectivity at data rates sufficient for video streaming. The prototype also surfaced an unintended consequence: BlueWalker 3 appeared among the fifty brightest objects in the night sky under certain solar angles, generating a [study published in *Nature*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06672-7) that influenced AST's optical reflectivity mitigation approach for subsequent generations.

## The Doppler and Interference Problems

Operating in standard cellular bands from a platform moving at approximately 7.5 kilometres per second introduces two intertwined engineering problems that do not arise in geostationary satellite communications. At 2 GHz, orbital velocity produces a peak frequency offset of roughly ±50 kHz—beyond the tolerance of an unmodified LTE or 5G modem without correction. AST's approach, codified across its patent families and later aligned with 3GPP Release 17 and 18 NR-NTN specifications, places the Doppler pre-correction burden entirely on the satellite. The payload computes and applies a frequency offset that anticipates the shift each handset will experience, so that by the time the signal arrives at the phone, it falls within the modem's acceptable error window. The satellite's digital signal processor must execute this calculation continuously and independently for every simultaneous user beam.

The second constraint is terrestrial interference. AST SpaceMobile shares spectrum with its MNO partners—the same low-band and mid-band frequencies used by AT&T's 850 MHz network in the United States, Verizon's equivalent bands, and Vodafone's European allocations. A satellite beam with an uncontrolled footprint risks interfering with cell towers below in high-density areas. The company's beam-steering algorithms form tight spot beams so that each illuminates only the geographic zone where service is needed: where terrestrial coverage is dense, beams are withheld; where a user sits in a coverage gap, the beam is precisely directed. The patent literature describes configurations supporting hundreds of discrete simultaneous cells per satellite.

## The AST5000 ASIC: Proprietary Silicon as Structural Moat

Processing ten gigahertz of phased-array bandwidth in real time—while simultaneously executing beam steering, Doppler pre-compensation, and handover logic for thousands of users—cannot be accomplished with commercial off-the-shelf electronics rated for the radiation environment of LEO. AST SpaceMobile spent an estimated [$45 million and approximately 150 engineer-years](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240327367837/en/AST-SpaceMobile-ASIC-Chip-Enters-Tape-Out-Phase-in-Collaboration-with-TSMC) developing the AST5000, a proprietary application-specific integrated circuit that entered tape-out at TSMC in March 2024, designed in collaboration with Cadence's electronic design automation platform. The chip supports 10 GHz of processing bandwidth and enables each Block 2 satellite to manage more than 2,000 simultaneous coverage cells at peak data speeds of 120 Mbps per cell.

Because the AST5000 is proprietary and radiation-hardened for the LEO environment, any competitor seeking to replicate the full system architecture would face a multi-year silicon development programme of comparable cost and duration before reaching production. This structural feature converts what might otherwise be a temporarily defensible engineering lead into a more durable barrier: ramping a novel ASIC from concept to production takes years even for well-capitalised organisations. Avellan has been direct about what this manufacturing achievement represents:

> "Simply put, we are the first company in the history of commercial satellite manufacturing to produce satellites of our size and power at scale."

## The Patent Portfolio: Scope and Competitive Signal

AST SpaceMobile's patent programme began with those 2017 filings by Avellan and his chief scientist. The portfolio reached its 1,000th claim by [March 2021](https://ast-science.com/ast-and-science-announces-1000th-patent-claim/), a milestone the company publicly marked. The pace of filings accelerated through the BlueBird development cycle: by early 2024, total claims exceeded 3,100; by the [FY 2024 10-K filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm), the portfolio stood at more than 3,500 patent and patent-pending claims across 36 patent families worldwide, with approximately 1,050 officially granted or allowed as of mid-2024. Avellan is personally listed as co-inventor on 24 U.S. patents.

The most cited patent in the portfolio is [US9973266B1](https://patents.google.com/patent/US9973266B1/ko), "System and method for high throughput fractionated satellites (HTFS) for direct connectivity to and from end user devices and terminals using flight formations of small or very small satellites," which has received 96 forward citations from companies including Lynk Global and UbiquitiLink—direct competitors in the emerging direct-to-device sector. That citation pattern is diagnostic: the foundational architecture Avellan established has become the reference point against which later entrants must design around.

The 36 patent families span phased-array antenna design, large deployable structures, beam-forming and beam-steering algorithms, Doppler compensation methods, satellite-to-handset link-budget techniques, constellation management, interference coordination with terrestrial networks, and the satellite manufacturing processes required to fold, deploy, and verify arrays at production scale rather than in a prototype context.

## Block 2 and the Accumulating Aperture Advantage

BlueBird 6, the first Block 2 satellite, launched in December 2025 aboard an Indian LVM-3 rocket and [completed array unfolding in February 2026](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260210108166/en/AST-SpaceMobile-Successfully-Completes-Unfolding-of-BlueBird-6-the-Largest-Commercial-Communications-Array-Antenna-Ever-Deployed-in-Low-Earth-Orbit), deploying approximately 2,400 square feet of phased array—more than three times larger than the Block 1 arrays, and the third time in the company's history it had claimed the record for the largest commercial communications array in low Earth orbit. The successive aperture expansions from BlueWalker 3 to Block 1 to Block 2 reflect the systematic application of folding-mechanism patents, panel manufacturing processes, and deployment dynamics documented and protected across the portfolio.

Avellan has been consistent about the competitive consequence:

> "We are the only company capable of delivering 4G and 5G and in the future, 6G broadband speed sufficient for voice calls, voice over LTE, live video calls, streaming, and full Internet access directly to unmodified devices."

Whether that exclusivity holds as 3GPP Release 18 and 19 NR-NTN standards make the underlying technical specifications more widely legible is one of the central questions in the sector. What the patent estate, the AST5000 ASIC, and the cumulative manufacturing learning curve collectively represent—as of the May 2026 snapshot—is a multi-year head start in a capital-intensive, physics-constrained discipline where catching up requires not just money but time.

chapters.title: Block 2 execution, Starlink competition, capital structure, regulatory
chapters.body:
## Block 2 Deployment Execution

Five Block 1 satellites constitute a demonstration constellation, not a commercial network. The burden of proof rests on Block 2: substantially larger spacecraft targeted for deployment through 2025–2026.

The execution risks are layered. Block 2 satellites represent a meaningful step-change in satellite mass and complexity; manufacturing throughput at scale has historically been the single most common failure mode for novel LEO operators. AST's satellite production relies on a relatively small industrial base at its Midland, Texas facility and on component supply chains that include precision RF hardware. Any sustained bottleneck — whether in antenna assembly, phased-array electronics, or integration testing — would lengthen the gap between Block 1's proof-of-concept posture and the minimum-viable commercial footprint needed to serve AT&T, Verizon, and Vodafone subscribers at meaningful scale. The company has not disclosed a per-satellite manufacturing cost floor for Block 2, which limits external scrutiny of whether the unit economics pencil at the targeted capacity levels.

## Starlink Direct to Cell: Competitive Pressure from a Vertically Integrated Rival

SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell, partnered with T-Mobile, represents the sharpest competitive pressure. SpaceX can manufacture and launch hundreds of satellites per year on its own rockets at sub-market costs, and can cross-subsidise from Starlink broadband revenue. The counterargument: if Starlink DTC achieves "good enough" coverage at effectively zero incremental cost to T-Mobile subscribers, the case for MNOs to pay AST for a premium tier becomes harder to make. The competitive dynamic is further complicated by the fact that SpaceX remains AST's primary launch provider, creating a degree of dependency on a direct rival that has no structural parallel in the satellite industry.

## Capital Structure Adequacy Through Full Constellation

The adequacy question sharpens as Block 2 spending ramps. A full commercial constellation capable of continuous coverage across the 50-plus countries where AST holds MNO agreements would require dozens of Block 2 satellites; the capital intensity of that deployment, set against a revenue ramp that remains in its earliest innings, creates a funding gap that equity markets and existing partners must bridge. Equity dilution at current valuations is expensive; convertible instruments carry reset provisions and interest loads that accumulate during any deployment delay. Management has not provided a fully itemized total constellation cost figure in SEC filings, which leaves analysts modelling a range of scenarios. Investors who underwrote AST at its SPAC listing at an assumed target price must tolerate a longer-than-expected path to cash generation if Block 2 slips even modestly against schedule.

## Regulatory and Spectrum Coordination

AST SpaceMobile's architecture turns on a distinctive regulatory posture: rather than seeking its own global spectrum licences, it operates on spectrum already licensed to its MNO partners in each territory. This avoids the multi-decade ITU coordination battles that shaped legacy GEO satellite operators and the secondary market that has historically extracted rent from spectrum-scarce new entrants. On paper, it is an elegant solution. In practice, it disaggregates the regulatory problem into dozens of national approval processes, each requiring a regulator to sanction a space station transmitting on terrestrially-allocated bands in its jurisdiction.

Several major markets — including Japan, where Rakuten Mobile is an equity partner — have required bespoke regulatory filings and extended coordination periods. In-orbit frequency coordination with adjacent LEO constellations, particularly Starlink, adds a further dimension: the ITU coordination procedures for non-geostationary orbit systems are notoriously slow, and as the low-Earth orbit environment becomes more congested, interference avoidance agreements become harder to negotiate bilaterally. Any material regulatory delay in a Tier 1 market — the United States, Europe, India, Japan — compresses the near-term addressable revenue and undermines the "global coverage" story that underpins the MNO commercial pitches.

## MNO Partnership Commercial Conversion

The conversion risk is real. MNO agreements at this stage are typically structured around commercial milestones — minimum coverage thresholds, service-level commitments, pricing floors — that AST must hit before recurring per-subscriber or capacity revenue flows. An MNO operating under competitive pressure from fixed-wireless access, rival satellite entrants, or domestic spectrum auctions may elect to renegotiate terms, delay rollout, or, in an extreme case, substitute a competing direct-to-cell provider if the competitive landscape shifts. The revenue trajectory through 2024 — declining rather than growing as engineering services completed — illustrates how quickly the financial profile changes when milestone-based contributions end and subscriber-based revenue has not yet begun.

## Launch Service Availability and Cost

AST SpaceMobile's Block 1 deployment was executed entirely on SpaceX Falcon 9. The relationship has been productive but structurally uncomfortable: SpaceX's own Starlink DTC is a direct competitive product, and launch manifest access is ultimately allocated at SpaceX's commercial discretion. Falcon 9 pricing for dedicated rideshare is public and competitive, but dedicated large-batch manifests for a customer with a competing satellite service could, in principle, be deprioritised relative to Starlink's own internal launches.

AST has not publicly disclosed binding launch agreements for the full Block 2 constellation. Alternative launch providers — United Launch Alliance's Vulcan, Rocket Lab's Neutron (still in development as of mid-2026), and Arianespace — each carry either payload capacity constraints or uncertain pricing relative to Falcon 9. A meaningful delay in securing launch slots, or a step-up in launch cost per kilogramme, flows directly into the capital adequacy calculus above. The interdependence between deployment schedule, launch cost, and funding runway means that any adverse development in one variable propagates quickly through the others, compressing the margin for execution error that a pre-revenue company can absorb.

chapters.title: Block 2 deployment, commercial revenue conversion, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Block 2 Inflection

Block 2 is not an incremental upgrade — it is the architecture that makes direct-to-cell economics work at scale. The company frames it as the backbone of a financially self-sustaining network: the first generation whose economics could plausibly close. Manufacturing is underway in Midland, with launches through 2025–2026 building toward initial commercial coverage across priority equatorial and mid-latitude markets.

## MNO Revenue Conversion Mechanics

The revenue conversion challenge is geometric, not contractual. Five Block 1 satellites serve any given region for only minutes per day. Meaningful commercial revenue requires a constellation large enough to provide acceptable service continuity. The MNO partnerships are signed; spectrum is secured in most priority markets; engineering is validated. What remains is constellation scale to convert contracted agreements into cash receipts.

## Capital Structure and the 2025–2026 Funding Bridge

Strategic equity investments from AT&T and Google extended cash runway through the Block 2 launch window. The investor base has consolidated around strategic holders with long-duration interests — Vodafone, Rakuten, AT&T, Google — aligning incentives with execution. Convertible debt introduces refinancing risk in 2026–2027, a potential dilution source if deployment timelines extend.

## Starlink Direct to Cell: The Competitive Constraint

SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell reached commercial availability in 2025, placing a well-capitalised competitor in market ahead of AST's revenue ramp. The differentiation question: whether AST's carrier-agnostic model — aggregating subscribers across AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, and 50+ partners without replicating capital investment per relationship — proves commercially superior to Starlink's single-carrier approach. Competitive pressure creates urgency around Block 2 execution to avoid T-Mobile entrenching an early-mover advantage.

## 2026–2030: The Scaling Horizon

The five-year arc from 2026 through 2030 represented, in compressed form, the company's entire commercial thesis. A constellation adequate for initial commercial service — likely requiring several dozen Block 2 satellites in addition to the five Block 1 vehicles — was the minimum condition for material revenue recognition. A full global coverage build-out of the scale envisioned in FCC filings, eventually extending to several hundred satellites, was the precondition for the wholesale capacity model to generate operating leverage.

| Milestone | Constellation Scale | Commercial Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Block 2 initial deployment | ~20–30 satellites | Coverage continuity for first commercial billing wave |
| Phase I completion | ~90+ satellites | Adequate equatorial and tropical commercial coverage |
| Phase II build-out | ~168+ satellites | Expanded mid-latitude coverage; US service continuity |
| Full global constellation | 240+ satellites | Near-global MNO revenue at scale |

The financial model embedded in analyst projections through 2024 anticipated a steep revenue ramp beginning in 2025–2026 as Block 2 satellites became operational, with the company potentially approaching operating break-even sometime in the 2027–2028 window under base-case assumptions — assumptions that required no significant launch failures, no material deterioration in MNO partner commitments, and a capital markets environment that would support at least one further equity raise if deployment timelines slipped.

For Avellan, who had founded the company in Midland, Texas in 2017 with the explicit thesis that existing unmodified smartphones were already radio-compatible with a sufficiently large low-orbit phased array, the 2026–2030 horizon was not speculative territory. It was the execution phase of an engineering proposition that BlueWalker 3 had validated in September 2022 and Block 1 had confirmed in the autumn of 2024. Whether the commercial build-out could proceed at the pace the capital structure required — and far enough ahead of a Starlink Direct to Cell competitor with substantially deeper resources — remained the central, unresolved question facing the company at the frozen snapshot date.

## C. Technology Glossary

**BlueBird** — AST SpaceMobile's operational satellite series. Block 1 comprises the first five commercial-grade spacecraft. Block 2 satellites carry substantially larger phased-array antennas for higher per-satellite throughput.

**BlueWalker 3** — The prototype satellite launched September 2022 that demonstrated direct-to-cell voice and broadband data from LEO to unmodified commercial handsets.

**Phased-array antenna** — The large unfurled antenna array aboard each BlueBird satellite that enables direct connection to standard smartphones on existing LTE 4G/5G cellular bands without hardware modification at the handset.

**Direct-to-cell (DTC)** — Service architecture in which a satellite provides cellular connectivity to standard mobile handsets using spectrum licensed by a partner mobile network operator, bypassing terrestrial base-station infrastructure.
